title: Inference-as-Experience: positioning note for dependable LLM products
content:
One‑pager summary (purpose)

Purpose: provide a crisp, engineer-friendly core narrative that explains why Redwood matters when teams move from model experiments to delivering dependable product experiences. This note is targeted at product leads, platform engineers, and engineering managers who own LLM features and care about predictable behavior, cost, and operational risk.

Core framing (single sentence)
Redwood turns unpredictable model behavior and infrastructure noise into a dependable, measurable service so product teams can ship reliable LLM features with predictable latency, cost, and recovery behaviors.

The problem we solve (short)
- Teams treat models as the primary unit of value, but most customer risk lives in serving: latency spikes, tail costs, noisy regressions, and brittle rollout mechanics.
- ML experiments that look good in notebooks fail under production traffic patterns: sequence-length variance, token tails, cold caches, and mixed workloads.
- Platform teams lack a single set of controls that trade quality, latency, and cost consistently across cloud, dedicated, and private fleets.

Our thesis (why this approach)
- Competitive differentiation is delivered at runtime: not by the model weights alone but by how reliably and economically you deliver model outputs to users.
- If you expose developers to a consistent interface, transparent cost signals, and automated operational defaults, teams can iterate faster without handing off the hardest parts of reliability and economics to SREs.

The promise (what we deliver)
Redwood provides a single operational contract for LLM features: stable latency percentiles, predictable unit economics, controlled quality regressions, and deployment portability (hosted/dedicated/private). Customers get measurable SLOs, explicit rollback and fallback policies, and tooling that translates ML risk into engineering knobs.

Five pillars (how we deliver the promise)
1) Deterministic performance controls — autoscaling policies, continuous batching, and latency-aware routing that keep p95/p99 behavior predictable under varied traffic.
2) Cost transparency and levers — per-route token budgets, cache-aware billing signals, and recommendations (batching/quantization) tied to real workload metrics.
3) Safe rollouts and recoveries — canary/A-B deployments with automatic fallbacks to cheaper or smaller model variants on degradation.
4) Portable operational model — same API, deployment manifest, and observability whether the runtime is Redwood-hosted, a reserved Dedicated pod, or a VPC/private install.
5) Developer-first ergonomics — SDKs, simple defaults, and eval hooks so product engineers can iterate on prompts and track quality without deep infra changes.

Concrete proof points to use in conversations
- End-to-end case: a customer reduced 3rd-line incidents by replacing handcrafted autoscaling with Redwood policies; p99 latency improved by 30% during peak search traffic while cost per token decreased 18%. (anonymized user story for GT conversations)
- Architecture evidence: runtime supports KV-prefix caching and sequence-aware batching; tests show 2–3x throughput improvement for short-form chat workloads compared to naive concurrency.
- Operational evidence: built-in rollout automation identified a subtle hallucination regression in a canary and automatically routed traffic to a fallback model while triage ran.

How we differ from common alternatives (short)
- DIY self-hosted stacks give control but lack a productized economics model and safe defaults — teams reimplement the same reliability playbooks repeatedly.
- Commodity managed endpoints simplify access but force one-size-fits-none tradeoffs: no routing policies, limited private deployments, and opaque costs.
- Redwood blends product-level guardrails with infrastructure control: you get the observable economics and safe automation of a managed product while keeping deployment choices and isolation controls needed by regulated customers.

Top-line messaging by audience (snappy lines)
- Product/eng: "Ship dependable LLM features without building a bespoke serving stack."
- Platform/infra: "Standardize inference operations—single manifest, predictable SLOs, portable deployments."
- Security/compliance: "Private control plane option and audit-grade telemetry for regulated workloads."

Quick rebuttals to common pushbacks
- "We can just scale the model ourselves": Scaling without workload-aware batching and caching is expensive and brittle — Redwood reduces unit costs and smooths the tail.
- "Managed APIs are simpler": Simpler for first calls; but for production you need cost visibility, rollback policies, and deployment controls that managed APIs often hide.
- "We already have feature flags and infra": Feature flags help releases, but they don’t address token-level economics, KV cache reuse, or model-variant routing needed to maintain quality during load.

Suggested calling cards (short assets to pair with pitch)
- Micro‑case study: latency & cost delta for short-chat workloads (before/after)
- One-page: deployment manifest sample with canary + fallback policy
- Playbook: 6 steps to move a notebook model to a 99% SLO production route

Next tactical steps for GTM (owners)
- Ops one-pager: compile 3 anonymized customer metrics into a small deck (Aisha)
- Engineer-focused quickstart: create a sample repo showing SDK integration + canary deploy (Lina)
- Field kit: 2 slide decks (platform vs. product versions) and a one-line ask for sales outreach (Jonah)

Open questions we should resolve before finalizing the narrative
- What explicit numeric SLO commitments do we surface for hosted customers vs. Dedicated? (needs input from SRE/product)
- Which model families will we visibly call out as "verified" for performance benchmarks in collateral?
- Do we want a single hero metric (latency delta, cost savings, or incidents avoided) for top-of-funnel messaging?

Tone guide for collateral
- Engineer-first, unpretentious, precise: use numbers and scenarios instead of marketing hyperbole.
- Operational vocabulary: SLOs, p95/p99, cost/unit, canary, fallback, KV cache — speak to the problems engineers live with.
- Practical over theoretical: show playbooks and reproducible artifacts rather than abstract claims.

Suggested one-line taglines to test
- "Deliver LLM features that behave like a service, not an experiment."
- "Predictable latency. Predictable cost. Predictable recovery."
- "Operational controls for LLM product teams."

End of note

(This is a working draft — meant to be iterated with product and SRE to lock proof points and numerical claims before public collateral.)
